decks.title: The Philosophy of the Constitution, Part 1: Ideals, Freedom, Justice, Diversity and Secularism
goals: Explain what the philosophy of a constitution means and how a constitution reflects moral values
Describe a constitution as a means of democratic transformation and as a limit on power
Name the ideals of the Preamble and the dated note on the 42nd Amendment (1976)
Explain individual freedom, social justice and respect for diversity and minority rights
Define secularism and contrast the Indian model with strict separation

slides.heading: The Philosophy of the Constitution
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **ideals** behind the Constitution, and four core features: **freedom**, **social justice**, **diversity** and **secularism**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what philosophy means, the Preamble ideals, freedom and social justice, diversity, and secularism
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A constitution is more than a list of rules. Behind every provision there is an idea of what is right. In this part we ask what ideals lie behind the Indian Constitution, and we study four of its core features: individual freedom, social justice, respect for diversity, and secularism.

slides.heading: What is the philosophy of a constitution?

rows: Constitution
The basic document that sets up the institutions of a state, states their powers and the rights of citizens
Philosophy of a constitution
The ideals and moral values behind its provisions, which explain why the provisions take the form they do
Approach
Ask what values a provision serves and what kind of society it hopes to build
Source
The Constituent Assembly debates help us to see the ideals and reasons of the members

visual.alt: Table of terms: a constitution is the basic document that sets up institutions and states powers and rights; the philosophy of a constitution is the ideals and moral values behind its provisions; the approach is to ask what values a provision serves; the Constituent Assembly debates are a source for the ideals and reasons of the members

slides.narration: A constitution is the basic document that sets up the institutions of a state, states their powers, and lays down the rights of citizens. The philosophy of a constitution is the set of ideals and moral values behind its provisions. To study it, we ask what values a provision serves and what kind of society it hopes to build.

slides.heading: Three roles of a constitution

rows: Reflects moral values
Its choices show what a society holds to be right
The editorial of Tarsia reads its constitution as a vision of dignity
Means of democratic transformation
Changes an unequal society by lawful and peaceful means
Brendale opens its wells to the Lowrens
Limits power
Binds those who govern, even a majority
Norvale requires a hearing before a judge

visual.alt: Table of the roles of a constitution: it reflects moral values, as in the editorial of imagined Tarsia; it is a means of democratic transformation, as when imagined Brendale opens its wells to the Lowrens; and it limits power, as when imagined Norvale requires a hearing before a judge

slides.narration: A constitution reflects the moral values of a society. It can be a means of democratic transformation, changing an unequal society by lawful and peaceful means. And it limits power, binding those who govern, even a government with a majority. Imagined Brendale, Tarsia and Norvale show each of these roles.

slides.narration: The Preamble sets out four ideals. Justice is social, economic and political. Liberty covers thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. Equality is of status and of opportunity. Fraternity assures the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation. Together they show the values the Constitution wishes to realise.

slides.heading: The Preamble: key words and a dated note

Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic
Justice
Social, economic and political
Liberty
Of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
Equality
Of status and of opportunity
Fraternity
Assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation
Dated note
Socialist, secular and integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976)

visual.alt: Table of the key words of the Preamble: the nature of the state is sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and republic; justice is social, economic and political; liberty is of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; equality is of status and of opportunity; fraternity assures the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation; the words socialist, secular and integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment of 1976

slides.narration: The Preamble describes the state as sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and a republic. A dated note: the words socialist, secular and integrity were added by the forty second Amendment in nineteen seventy six. Justice, liberty, equality and fraternity were part of the Preamble from the start.

slides.narration: The debates of the Constituent Assembly are a source for understanding the ideals behind the Constitution. Some stressed the liberty of the individual, others the removal of social inequality, and many sought a balance. We read the debates together with the text.

slides.narration: This web shows the core features of the political philosophy. They are individual freedom, social justice, respect for diversity and minority rights, secularism of the Indian kind, universal adult franchise, federalism with special provisions, and one national identity. In this part we study the first four. The rest follow in Part two.

slides.heading: Individual freedom

rows: Meaning
Each person is free to think, speak and act within limits fixed by law
Examples
Freedom of expression; protection against arbitrary arrest (Articles 19 and 22)
Why it matters
It keeps the power of the state in check and respects the dignity of the person
Imagined case
A trader of Mirenia is held for days without a reason or a hearing: the practice conflicts with this value

visual.alt: Table on individual freedom: each person is free to think, speak and act within limits fixed by law; examples are freedom of expression and protection against arbitrary arrest under Articles 19 and 22; it keeps state power in check and respects dignity; an imagined trader of Mirenia held without reason or hearing shows a conflict with the value

slides.narration: Individual freedom means that each person is free to think, speak and act within limits fixed by law. Examples are freedom of expression and protection against arbitrary arrest. This value keeps the power of the state in check. If a trader is held for days without a reason or a hearing, the practice conflicts with this value.

slides.heading: Social justice

rows: Meaning
Fair treatment of every group in society, including the removal of long-standing exclusion
Means
Special provisions such as reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
Aim
Equality of opportunity: a fair chance for those who started far behind
Seen by some
As a means to equality, and not as a departure from it

visual.alt: Table on social justice: fair treatment of every group, including removal of long-standing exclusion; means such as reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; the aim of equality of opportunity; seen by some as a means to equality and not a departure from it

slides.narration: Social justice means fair treatment of every group in society, including the removal of long standing exclusion. One means is reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, which aims at equality of opportunity. Many see such provisions as a means to equality, and not as a departure from it.

slides.heading: Respect for diversity and minority rights

headers: Respect for diversity and minority rights
rows: Meaning
Different religions, languages and cultures are recognised and protected
Community-based rights
Rights held by communities, such as religious and linguistic minorities, beside individual rights
Example
The right of minorities to run educational institutions (Article 30)
Imagined case
A language community of Orwen runs schools that teach in its mother tongue

visual.alt: Table on diversity and minority rights: different religions, languages and cultures are recognised and protected; community-based rights, such as those of minorities, stand beside individual rights; for example the right of minorities to run educational institutions under Article 30; an imagined language community of Orwen runs schools in its mother tongue

slides.narration: The Constitution respects diversity. It recognises community based rights, such as the rights of religious and linguistic minorities, beside the rights of individuals. For example, minorities may run their own educational institutions. In imagined Orwen, a language community runs schools that teach in its mother tongue.

slides.heading: Secularism: a standard definition

rows: Secularism
The principle that the state does not identify itself with any one religion and treats all believers and non-believers equally
Strict separation
State and religion are kept completely apart, with no help to or interference in religion
Principled distance
A distance kept from every religion on a principle of equal respect, which allows reform or support where equality requires
Examples of intervention
A law against untouchability; equal grants to institutions of all faiths

visual.alt: Table of terms: secularism is the principle that the state does not identify with any one religion and treats all believers and non-believers equally; strict separation keeps state and religion completely apart; principled distance is a distance kept from every religion on a principle of equal respect, which allows reform or support where equality requires; examples are a law against untouchability and equal grants to institutions of all faiths

slides.narration: Secularism is the principle that the state does not identify itself with any one religion and treats all believers and non believers equally. Strict separation keeps state and religion completely apart. The Indian model keeps a principled distance from every religion, and the state may reform or support communities equally where equality requires.

notes.title: The Philosophy of the Constitution: Notes

sections.heading: 1. What is the philosophy of a constitution?
sections.body_md:
A **constitution** is the basic document that sets up the institutions of a state, states their powers and the rights of citizens. The **philosophy of a constitution** is the set of **ideals and moral values** behind its provisions. A constitution can **reflect moral values**, be a **means of democratic transformation** (changing an unequal society by lawful means) and **limit power** (bind those who govern, even a majority).

The **debates of the Constituent Assembly** are a source for the ideals and reasons of the members, read together with the text.

The ideals and moral values behind its provisions, which explain why they take the form they do.
The change of an unequal society towards equality by lawful and peaceful means under a constitution.

sections.heading: 2. The Preamble and its ideals
sections.body_md:
The Preamble describes the state as **sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and a republic**. Its ideals are **justice** (**social, economic and political**), **liberty** (of **thought, expression, belief, faith and worship**), **equality** (of **status and of opportunity**) and **fraternity** (assuring the **dignity of the individual** and the **unity and integrity of the nation**).

**Dated note:** the words **socialist, secular and integrity** were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.

key_terms.definition_md: The ideal of fairness in society, in economic life and in public affairs: social, economic and political.
The ideal of freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
The ideal of equal standing for every person (status) and a fair chance to develop (opportunity).
The ideal of a sense of belonging together that assures the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation.

sections.heading: 3. Individual freedom and social justice
sections.body_md:
**Individual freedom:** each person is free to think, speak and act within limits fixed by law. Examples: **freedom of expression** and **protection against arbitrary arrest** (Articles 19 and 22).

**Social justice:** fair treatment of every group, including the removal of long-standing exclusion. **Reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes** are a means to **equality of opportunity**.

key_terms.definition_md: The value that each person is free to think, speak and act within limits fixed by law.
Fair treatment of every group in society, including the removal of long-standing exclusion.
A provision that sets aside a share of seats or posts for certain groups as a means to equality of opportunity.

sections.heading: 4. Diversity, minority rights and secularism
sections.body_md:
The Constitution **respects diversity** and recognises **community-based rights**, such as the right of religious and linguistic minorities to **run educational institutions** (Article 30), beside individual rights.

**Secularism** is the principle that the state does not identify itself with any one religion and treats all believers and non-believers equally. The **Indian model** keeps a **principled distance** from all religions: the state may **intervene to reform** (for example against untouchability) or **support communities equally**, unlike strict separation. Secularism is studied in depth in a later chapter.

key_terms.definition_md: Rights of religious and linguistic minorities, for example to run their own educational institutions.
Rights held by communities and not only by individuals.
The principle that the state does not identify with any one religion and treats all believers and non-believers equally.
The Indian way of keeping apart from every religion on a principle of equal respect, which allows reform or equal support.

sections.heading: 5. Franchise, federalism, identity and procedure
sections.body_md:
**Universal adult franchise** gives every adult citizen the vote, with no test of wealth, schooling, caste, gender or religion (Article 326). It was adopted **from the start**, a **bold step** beside the **gradual extension** of the vote in many Western countries. The voting age was 21 years, lowered to **18 years** by the **61st Amendment (1988)**.

**Federalism** shares power between the Union and the states, with **special provisions** for some states (**Article 371** and related Articles): **asymmetric** arrangements. There is **one national identity** beside regional, linguistic and religious identities.

**Procedural achievements:** **faith in deliberation**, a **spirit of compromise and accommodation**, and **consensus** wherever possible.

An arrangement in which not all units of a federation are treated alike, because some have special provisions.

Agreement of all or nearly all members, reached by discussion, instead of a bare majority.

sections.heading: 6. Criticisms and replies
sections.body_md:
Critics have argued that the Constitution is:

- **Unwieldy**: very long and detailed. **Reply:** the length reflects India's needs, and much detail is usual.
- **Unrepresentative**: the Assembly was elected on a **limited franchise** and not by universal adult franchise. **Reply:** its members held **diverse opinions** and the **debates were open**.
- **Alien**: many provisions were **borrowed**. **Reply:** ideas were **adapted** to Indian conditions and to the **ideals of the national movement**.

Students should weigh each reply with reasons.

key_terms.definition_md: The criticism that the Constitution is too long and detailed to be easily followed.
The criticism that the Constituent Assembly, elected on a limited franchise, did not speak for everyone.
The criticism that the Constitution is foreign because many of its provisions were borrowed.

sections.heading: 7. Limitations
sections.body_md:
The textbook notes three limitations:

- A **centralised notion of national unity**.
- Some issues of **gender justice**, for example **within the family**, were **not fully addressed**.
- Some **social and economic rights** were placed in the **Directive Principles** and not among the **Fundamental Rights**.

A fair account weighs these limitations against the achievements, with reasons.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Quoting the Preamble from memory: name the ideals and give their meaning in your own words.
- Saying the 42nd Amendment added justice or liberty: it added socialist, secular and integrity in 1976.
- Saying Indian secularism is strict separation: it is a principled distance, with reform and equal support.
- Giving a criticism without its reply, or taking a side on a debated point: write critics have argued, give the reply, then weigh with reasons.
- Confusing the vote and the Assembly: universal adult franchise was adopted from the start, while the Assembly was elected on a limited franchise.

**Tips:** support each feature with an example; pair every criticism with a reply; give dates (1976, 1988); use imagined cases for comparisons.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the philosophy of a constitution?

options.text_md: The list of all its Articles in numerical order
The ideals and moral values that lie behind its provisions and give them direction
The legal procedure by which it can be amended
The history of the court cases decided under it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The ideals and moral values that lie behind its provisions and give them direction. The philosophy of a constitution is the set of ideals and values that its provisions are meant to serve. A list of Articles, an amendment procedure and a record of cases deal with its text, its change and its use, not with the ideals behind it.

questions.stem_md: An editorial in the imagined newspaper Tarsia Daily argues that the national constitution is more than a rule book for officials, because its choices about equality and dignity show what kind of society Tarsia wants to become. This editorial treats a constitution as

options.text_md: a purely technical manual of office procedures
a record of past court cases
a document that matters only to lawyers
a statement of moral values and a vision of the society a people wish to build

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a statement of moral values and a vision of the society a people wish to build. The editorial reads the choices in the document as expressions of values, so it sees a constitution as a moral and social vision. A technical manual, a case record or a lawyers' text would not carry such a meaning for ordinary citizens.

questions.stem_md: A clause in the constitution of the imagined republic of Norvale says that no minister may order a person to be locked up unless the person is brought before a judge within a fixed number of days. Which purpose of a constitution does this clause mainly serve?

options.text_md: Limiting the power of those who govern, even when they enjoy a majority
Increasing the powers of the police
Fixing the date of the next election
Choosing the national anthem

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Limiting the power of those who govern, even when they enjoy a majority. A rule that binds ministers protects individuals against the arbitrary use of authority, which is the limiting function of a constitution. The clause does not enlarge police powers, and it has nothing to do with election dates or anthems.

questions.stem_md: Before the new constitution of the imagined society of Brendale, members of a community called the Lowrens were not allowed to draw water from common wells. The constitution declares such exclusion unlawful and gives the Lowrens an equal place in public life. This shows a constitution used as

options.text_md: a tool to keep the old ranks unchanged
a way of ending all elections
a means of democratic transformation of an unequal society
a treaty with a foreign power

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a means of democratic transformation of an unequal society. A document that removes long-standing exclusion and opens an equal place to all is working to change society by peaceful, lawful means, which is democratic transformation. Keeping the old ranks, ending elections or signing a treaty would not match what the clause does.

questions.stem_md: Why do students of political theory read the debates of the Constituent Assembly when they study the philosophy of the Constitution?

options.text_md: The debates replace the text of the Constitution
The debates record the results of later elections
The debates show the ideals and reasoning that members offered for its provisions
The debates list the prices of goods in 1949

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The debates show the ideals and reasoning that members offered for its provisions. Members explained why they wished a provision to take a certain form, so the debates help a reader to see the ideals behind the text. They do not replace the text, and they are not a record of later elections or prices.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following correctly lists the words that describe the nature of the Indian state in the Preamble?

options.text_md: Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic
Sovereign, federal, theocratic, democratic, republic
Independent, socialist, secular, oligarchic, monarchy
Sovereign, capitalist, secular, democratic, republic

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic. The five words are sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and republic. The other lists bring in words such as theocratic, oligarchic, monarchy or capitalist, which the Preamble does not use to describe the state.

questions.stem_md: Which set of words was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976)?

options.text_md: Sovereign, democratic and republic
Justice, liberty and equality
Fraternity and dignity
Socialist, secular and integrity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Socialist, secular and integrity. The 42nd Amendment added socialist, secular and integrity. Sovereign, democratic and republic, as well as justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, were part of the Preamble from the start.

questions.stem_md: A clause in the imagined constitution of Zandria says that every worker shall be paid a wage on which a family can live decently. Under which ideal of the Indian Preamble would such a clause be placed?

options.text_md: Political justice
Economic justice
Liberty of worship
Unity and integrity of the nation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Economic justice. A clause about wages and a decent living concerns fairness in economic life, which is economic justice. Political justice is about a voice in public affairs, liberty of worship about faith, and unity and integrity about the nation as a whole.

questions.stem_md: A clause in the imagined constitution of Mirenia says that no one may be punished for peacefully holding or sharing an opinion. Which Preamble ideal does it express?

options.text_md: Liberty of thought and expression
Equality of status
Economic justice
Fraternity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Liberty of thought and expression. Protection for the peaceful holding and sharing of opinions is liberty of thought and expression. Equality of status, economic justice and fraternity deal with standing, livelihood and belonging.

questions.stem_md: The imagined charter of Halcor asks every school to teach the shared story of all its communities, so that children of different communities feel that they belong together. Which Preamble ideal is this closest to?

options.text_md: Liberty of faith
Fraternity
Political justice
Equality of opportunity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Fraternity. Teaching people to feel that they belong together builds the sense of common life that fraternity stands for. Liberty of faith, political justice and equality of opportunity concern other matters.

questions.stem_md: Two equally able students of the imagined town of Brenmark compete for a college seat. One belongs to a community that was kept out of schools for generations. A scheme sets aside some seats for that community. Which ideal does the scheme mainly try to advance?

options.text_md: Liberty of worship
Sovereignty of the state
Equality of opportunity
The republican form of government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Equality of opportunity. The scheme gives members of a long-excluded community a fair chance to compete, which is equality of opportunity. Worship, sovereignty and the republican form are not what such a scheme addresses.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly distinguishes equality of status from equality of opportunity?

options.text_md: Status refers to equal wealth; opportunity refers to equal votes
Status refers to equal marks in examinations; opportunity refers to equal jobs for everyone
There is no difference between the two
Status refers to equal standing before the law and in society; opportunity refers to a fair chance to develop and compete

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Status refers to equal standing before the law and in society; opportunity refers to a fair chance to develop and compete. Equality of status is about the equal standing of persons, and equality of opportunity is about a fair chance for each to make use of their abilities. They do not mean equal wealth, equal marks or equal jobs, and the two are not the same.

questions.stem_md: Fraternity, as an ideal of the Preamble, is said to assure two things. They are

options.text_md: the wealth of the individual and the size of the nation
the speed of justice and the number of states
the freedom of the press and the strength of the army
the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation. Fraternity is linked with respect for each person and with the oneness of the nation. Wealth, size, speed of justice, number of states, the press and the army are not what the ideal is said to assure.

questions.stem_md: The police of the imagined province of Mirenia keep a trader in a lock-up for many days without telling him why and without taking him before a magistrate. Which feature of the political philosophy of the Indian Constitution speaks most directly against such a practice?

options.text_md: Universal adult franchise
Asymmetric federalism
Individual freedom, including protection against arbitrary arrest
A common national identity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Individual freedom, including protection against arbitrary arrest. Holding a person without reasons or a hearing is an arbitrary use of power, which the commitment to individual freedom, with its protection against arbitrary arrest, rules out. Franchise, federal arrangements and national identity are not the values at stake.

questions.stem_md: A scheme in the imagined state of Delvar sets aside a share of seats in public colleges for communities that were shut out of education for generations. Supporters call it a path to equal opportunity. Which value of the Constitution's philosophy does the scheme express?

options.text_md: Secularism
Social justice
Federalism
Universal franchise

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Social justice. Special provisions for groups that suffered long exclusion, meant to widen their opportunities, express social justice. They are not an example of secularism, federalism or the franchise.

questions.stem_md: According to the usual textbook account, why does the Constitution provide reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?

options.text_md: As a means of securing equality of opportunity for groups that suffered long exclusion
To give them a permanent separate state
To end the principle of equality
To remove them from general elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** As a means of securing equality of opportunity for groups that suffered long exclusion. Reservations are presented as a way to give long-excluded groups a fair chance, so they serve equality of opportunity. They do not set up separate states, they do not abandon equality, and they do not remove anyone from general elections.

questions.stem_md: A linguistic minority in the imagined state of Orwen wishes to start and run its own schools to teach in its mother tongue. Which constitutional idea supports the community in doing so?

options.text_md: The rule that every school must be run by the state
The recognition of minority rights, including the right to run educational institutions
The residuary powers of the Union
The adult franchise

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The recognition of minority rights, including the right to run educational institutions. The Constitution recognises the rights of religious and linguistic minorities to run educational institutions of their choice. A state monopoly on schools would deny this right, and residuary powers and the franchise concern other matters.

questions.stem_md: What is distinctive about the approach of the Indian Constitution to rights, in the textbook account?

options.text_md: It recognises only the rights of individuals
It recognises only the rights of communities
It leaves every right to be decided by ordinary state laws
It recognises the rights of communities, such as minorities, alongside the rights of individuals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It recognises the rights of communities, such as minorities, alongside the rights of individuals. The textbook account points out that the Constitution gives community-based rights, such as those of minorities, together with individual rights. It does not limit itself to either kind alone, and it does not leave rights to ordinary state laws.

questions.stem_md: Which statement gives a standard definition of secularism?

options.text_md: The principle that the state keeps apart from any one religion, favours none and is hostile to none, and treats all believers and non-believers equally
The principle that the state adopts the religion of the majority
The principle that religion is banned from all public life
The principle that religious leaders rule the state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The principle that the state keeps apart from any one religion, favours none and is hostile to none, and treats all believers and non-believers equally. Secularism means that the state does not identify itself with any one religion and treats everyone equally whatever their belief. Adopting the majority faith, banning religion, or rule by religious leaders would each go against that principle.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Veldora keeps religion entirely out of public life: it never funds or helps a religious body and never interferes in a religious practice. The imagined state of Tarsia keeps a principled distance, supports the institutions of all faiths on equal terms, and may pass laws to end practices that deny equality. Which pairing is correct?

options.text_md: Veldora follows the Indian model; Tarsia follows strict separation
Both follow strict separation
Veldora follows strict separation, typical of the Western model; Tarsia follows a model like the Indian one
Neither can be called secular

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Veldora follows strict separation, typical of the Western model; Tarsia follows a model like the Indian one. Complete non-involvement and no support for any religious body is strict separation, the typical Western pattern. Equal support for all faiths, together with the power to intervene to reform, is the mark of the Indian model, so the other pairings reverse or deny this.

questions.stem_md: The government of the imagined state of Kalmar offers repair grants to school buildings run by trusts of several religions, on the same terms to each. Which feature of Indian secularism does this show?

options.text_md: The state establishes one religion as official
The state bans religious schools
The state may support communities equally instead of keeping strict separation
The state never has any dealings with religious bodies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The state may support communities equally instead of keeping strict separation. Equal grants to institutions of different faiths show support given without preference, which is allowed in the Indian model. An official religion, a ban on religious schools, or total non-involvement would be different arrangements.

questions.stem_md: A law of the imagined state of Orwen forbids the managers of a shrine to turn away people because of the community into which they were born. Which feature of the Indian model of secularism does this illustrate?

options.text_md: The state may step in to reform religious practices that deny equality
The state never interferes in religion
The state favours one religion over others
Religion has no place in the life of the people

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The state may step in to reform religious practices that deny equality. A law that ends exclusion on grounds of birth shows the state intervening to reform a practice, as it did against untouchability. This differs from non-interference, from favouring one faith, or from denying religion any place in life.

questions.stem_md: The imagined republic of Brenmark announces that all its adults shall vote under a system of universal adult franchise. Which description of this system is correct?

options.text_md: The right to vote only for owners of property
The right to vote only for educated citizens
The right to vote only for men
The right of every adult citizen to vote, whatever their wealth, education, caste, gender or religion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The right of every adult citizen to vote, whatever their wealth, education, caste, gender or religion. Universal adult franchise gives the vote to every adult citizen without tests of property, learning, caste, gender or faith. The other options describe restricted voting rights of the kind found in older systems.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country of Halcor the vote was given first to men who owned land, later to all men, and only after many decades to women. The imagined country Mirenia gave every adult the vote at its very first election, though most voters had never been to school. What made the approach of Mirenia bold?

options.text_md: It gave the vote only to educated people
It trusted all adult citizens as equal members of the political community from the start, instead of extending the vote in stages
It abolished elections
It copied Halcor exactly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It trusted all adult citizens as equal members of the political community from the start, instead of extending the vote in stages. Granting the vote to everyone at once, in spite of poverty and lack of schooling, treated every adult as an equal citizen from the beginning, unlike the staged extension in Halcor. The other options describe restricted voting, no elections, or imitation of Halcor.

questions.stem_md: The Constitution contains special provisions for certain states, for example under Article 371 and related Articles, while other states have none of these provisions. This feature belongs to its approach to

options.text_md: federalism with asymmetric arrangements
a unitary system
strict secularism
a gradual extension of the vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** federalism with asymmetric arrangements. Different arrangements for different states are the sign of asymmetric federalism. A unitary system has no states of this kind, and secularism and the franchise are separate matters.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best expresses the idea of national identity in the philosophy of the Indian Constitution?

options.text_md: A national identity that replaces every other identity
One national identity that does not cancel regional, linguistic or religious identities
A national identity based on a single religion
The absence of any national identity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** One national identity that does not cancel regional, linguistic or religious identities. The Constitution presents a common national identity that sits beside other identities and does not erase them. Replacing all identities, basing identity on one religion, or having none would each depart from this idea.

questions.stem_md: A drafting committee of the imagined assembly of Zandria meets for many weeks, hears every member on a disputed clause, redrafts it to include part of each side's concern, and adopts it without a division. Which procedural achievement does this show?

options.text_md: Universal adult franchise
Judicial review
Faith in deliberation, a spirit of compromise and a search for consensus
Asymmetric federalism

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Faith in deliberation, a spirit of compromise and a search for consensus. Hearing all sides, redrafting to meet concerns and adopting the clause without a division are marks of deliberation, compromise and consensus. The franchise, judicial review and asymmetric federalism are different features.

questions.stem_md: In a debate at the imagined Lakemoor School, a student says that the Constitution has so many Articles, schedules and details that ordinary people find it hard to follow. Which criticism is this?

options.text_md: That it is unrepresentative
That it is alien
That it is silent on the franchise
That it is unwieldy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** That it is unwieldy. A complaint about length and detail is the criticism that the document is unwieldy. Unrepresentative refers to the way the Assembly was chosen, and alien refers to borrowed provisions.

questions.stem_md: A student of the imagined Lakemoor School replies to a critic by saying that, although the Constituent Assembly was chosen on a limited franchise, its members stood for many different opinions and its debates were open. Which criticism is being answered?

options.text_md: That the Constitution is unwieldy
That the Constitution is alien
That it left gender justice untouched
That the Constituent Assembly was unrepresentative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** That the Constituent Assembly was unrepresentative. A reply about the range of opinions and the open debates is aimed at the charge that the Assembly was not representative. The other criticisms would call for replies about length, borrowing or gender.

questions.stem_md: Critics have argued that the Constitution is alien because many of its provisions were borrowed. Which reply is commonly given?

options.text_md: No provision was borrowed from anywhere
Borrowed provisions were copied without change
Borrowed ideas were adapted to Indian conditions and to the ideals of the national movement
Borrowing is a defect that cannot be answered

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Borrowed ideas were adapted to Indian conditions and to the ideals of the national movement. The usual reply is that ideas from elsewhere were reshaped to fit Indian needs and the ideals of the national movement. Denying all borrowing, claiming exact copying, or conceding that no answer exists is not the reply put forward.

questions.stem_md: Some critics say that the Constitution rests on a centralised notion of national unity. Which of the following would they most likely cite in support?

options.text_md: The right of minorities to run schools
The strong powers given to the Union in relation to the states
The grant of the vote to all adults
Special provisions for some states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The strong powers given to the Union in relation to the states. A centralised idea of unity would be supported by strong Union powers. Minority rights, the adult franchise and special provisions for some states are often cited to show respect for diversity or equality, not centralisation.

questions.stem_md: Which limitation concerning gender justice is noted by some critics?

options.text_md: Issues of justice within the family were not fully addressed
Women were denied the vote at the start
The Constitution permitted untouchability
There is no right to equality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Issues of justice within the family were not fully addressed. The textbook account notes that some matters of gender justice inside the family were not fully addressed. Women did have the vote from the start, untouchability was abolished, and equality is a Fundamental Right.

questions.stem_md: A critic asks why a claim such as an adequate means of livelihood is a guiding principle for the state and not a right that a citizen can claim in court. Which limitation is the critic raising?

options.text_md: That the vote was limited at the start
That some social and economic rights were placed in the Directive Principles and not among the Fundamental Rights
That the Preamble is too long
That the Assembly borrowed too much

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** That some social and economic rights were placed in the Directive Principles and not among the Fundamental Rights. The critic asks why some social and economic rights sit in the Directive Principles, which are not enforceable in court, instead of the Fundamental Rights. The other options concern the franchise, the Preamble and borrowing.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A constitution can serve as a check on those who hold power.

**Reason (R):** It lays down rules that bind governments, even a government backed by a majority.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because the rules bind every government, a constitution can restrain the use of power.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Indian secularism requires a strict separation in which the state may never intervene in any religious matter.

**Reason (R):** The Indian state may intervene to reform religious practices that deny equality, and may support communities equally.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false, since the Indian model keeps a principled distance and does not demand strict separation. R is true and describes the actual position, which contradicts A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The words socialist and secular were part of the Preamble as adopted in 1949.

**Reason (R):** The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added the words socialist, secular and integrity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false, because those words were inserted in 1976. R is true, so the two statements contradict each other.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are presented as a means to equality of opportunity.

**Reason (R):** The Constitution allows no special provision of any kind for any group.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true, because reservations aim to widen the opportunities of long-excluded groups. R is false, since the Constitution does allow such special provisions.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Some critics have argued that the Constituent Assembly was not fully representative.

**Reason (R):** The Assembly was elected on a limited franchise and not by universal adult franchise.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the limited franchise behind the Assembly is the ground on which critics doubt that it spoke for everyone.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Constitution recognises community-based rights, such as those of religious and linguistic minorities, alongside individual rights.

**Reason (R):** Universal adult franchise was adopted from the start.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the franchise gives every adult a vote, whereas minority rights rest on respect for diversity and the protection of communities.

questions.stem_md: In the Indian model of secularism, the state must keep itself completely apart from religion and may never intervene in any religious practice.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The Indian model keeps a principled distance, and it allows the state to intervene to reform practices such as untouchability and to support communities equally.

questions.stem_md: The Constitution gave the vote to adult citizens from the start, without a test of property or education, whereas the vote was extended in stages in many Western countries.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Universal adult franchise from the beginning is regarded as a bold step when compared with the gradual extension of the vote in many Western countries.

questions.stem_md: According to critics who raise the question, every social and economic right is placed among the Fundamental Rights and none among the Directive Principles.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The criticism is just the opposite: some social and economic rights are placed in the Directive Principles instead.

questions.stem_md: The words socialist, secular and integrity were added to the Preamble by the ___ Amendment, passed in the year ___.
questions.solution_md: The 42nd Amendment, passed in 1976, made the addition.

questions.stem_md: The Preamble speaks of justice in three forms: social, ___ and political.
questions.solution_md: The three forms are social, economic and political justice.

questions.stem_md: Fraternity assures the ___ of the individual and the unity and ___ of the nation.
questions.solution_md: Fraternity is linked with the dignity of the individual and with the unity and integrity of the nation.

questions.stem_md: Match each ideal of the Preamble with what it covers.

options.text_md: Justice
Liberty
Equality
Fraternity

match_right.text_md: Of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
Dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the nation

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Justice has three forms, liberty five freedoms, equality two kinds, and fraternity two assurances.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined provision with the feature of the political philosophy that it expresses.

options.text_md: A province may not hold a person without a hearing before a magistrate
Seats set aside to widen the opportunities of long-excluded groups
A language community may run its own schools
The state gives equal grants to institutions of every faith

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Protection from arbitrary arrest is individual freedom, set-aside seats serve social justice, a language community's schools are a minority right, and equal grants show the Indian model of secularism.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these imagined stages in the extension of the vote in Halcor from the narrowest to the widest.

options.text_md: Every adult citizen may vote, with no test of property, sex or schooling
All men may vote, whatever their property
Men and women may vote, with some conditions
Only men with large landholdings may vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The vote widened from a few landholding men, to all men, to women with conditions, and finally to every adult without any test.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps in the order in which a disputed clause would ordinarily travel through the imagined assembly of Zandria.

options.text_md: The assembly adopts the clause, as far as possible by consensus
A compromise wording is drawn up to meet the main concerns
Members debate the clause in open session
A member proposes a clause for the draft

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). A proposal comes first, then open debate, then a compromise draft, and finally adoption by agreement.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the philosophy of a constitution? Give one example of an ideal found in the Indian Constitution.
questions.solution_md: The meaning and one ideal.

answer.model_answer_md: The **philosophy of a constitution** is the set of **ideals and moral values** that stand behind its provisions and explain their purpose. An example of such an ideal in the Indian Constitution is **justice**, together with liberty, equality and fraternity.

marking_scheme.step: Ideals and values behind its provisions
One correct ideal as an example

questions.stem_md: Using the imagined society of Brendale, whose constitution opens public wells to the Lowrens, explain how a constitution can be a means of democratic transformation.
questions.solution_md: Removing exclusion by lawful and peaceful means.

answer.model_answer_md: In Brendale, the constitution **removes an old exclusion** by lawful means and gives the Lowrens an **equal place**. A constitution can thus change an unequal society **peacefully**, through rules accepted by citizens, and not by force.

marking_scheme.step: Old exclusion removed by constitutional rule

questions.stem_md: A clause in the constitution of the imagined republic of Norvale requires every arrested person to be brought before a judge within a fixed number of days. How does it show that a constitution can limit power?
questions.solution_md: A rule that binds those in power.

answer.model_answer_md: The clause **binds the police and ministers** of Norvale. They cannot hold a person as they please. By placing a rule above those who govern, the constitution **protects the individual against arbitrary power**.

marking_scheme.step: The clause binds those who govern
It protects the individual against arbitrary use of power

questions.stem_md: Name the five words that describe the nature of the Indian state in the Preamble. Which of them were added by the 42nd Amendment?
questions.solution_md: Five words, and the additions of 1976.

answer.model_answer_md: The five words are **sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and republic**. The **42nd Amendment (1976)** added **socialist and secular**, as well as the word **integrity** in the phrase about the unity of the nation.

marking_scheme.step: Socialist and secular (and integrity) added in 1976

questions.stem_md: Explain in one or two lines each what liberty and equality mean as ideals of the Preamble.
questions.solution_md: Each ideal in one or two lines.

answer.model_answer_md: **Liberty** means freedom of **thought, expression, belief, faith and worship**. **Equality** means equality of **status** and of **opportunity**: equal standing for every person and a fair chance for each to develop.

marking_scheme.step: Equality of status and of opportunity

questions.stem_md: A linguistic minority of the imagined state of Orwen wishes to run its own schools. Why does the Constitution allow this, and what feature of its philosophy does this show?
questions.solution_md: The minority right and the feature it shows.

answer.model_answer_md: The Constitution recognises the **right of religious and linguistic minorities** to run educational institutions. This shows its **respect for diversity** and its recognition of **community-based rights** alongside the rights of individuals.

marking_scheme.step: Minorities may run their own educational institutions

questions.stem_md: Define secularism, and state in one line how the Indian model differs from strict separation of state and religion.
questions.solution_md: A definition and the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: **Secularism** is the principle that the state does not identify with any one religion and treats all believers and non-believers equally. In the **Indian model** the state keeps a **principled distance** and may **intervene to reform** or **support communities equally**, unlike strict separation.

marking_scheme.step: Principled distance; may reform or support equally, unlike strict separation

questions.stem_md: What is universal adult franchise? Why is its adoption from the start regarded as a bold step?
questions.solution_md: Definition and the contrast.

answer.model_answer_md: **Universal adult franchise** is the right of **every adult citizen to vote**, whatever property, schooling, caste, gender or religion. It is regarded as **bold** because in many Western countries the vote was **extended gradually** by stages.

marking_scheme.step: Every adult citizen may vote, without such tests
Bold when compared with the gradual extension in many Western countries

questions.stem_md: What is meant by asymmetric arrangements in federalism? Name one provision of the Indian Constitution that is cited as an example.
questions.solution_md: The meaning and one provision.

answer.model_answer_md: In **asymmetric federalism**, not all the units of a federation are treated alike, since some are given **special provisions** to suit their particular needs. In India, **Article 371 and related Articles** give such provisions to certain states.

marking_scheme.step: Some units have special provisions; not all alike

questions.stem_md: How does the Constitution view national identity in relation to regional and other identities?
questions.solution_md: One national identity beside others.

answer.model_answer_md: The Constitution holds that there can be **one national identity** along with **regional, linguistic and religious identities**. Belonging to the nation does not require a citizen to **give up** the other identities that matter to them.

marking_scheme.step: It exists alongside regional and other identities, not replacing them

questions.stem_md: State the procedural achievements that are credited to the way the Constitution was made.
questions.solution_md: Deliberation, compromise and consensus.

answer.model_answer_md: The procedural achievements are a **faith in deliberation**, a **spirit of compromise and accommodation**, and a wish to decide by **consensus** wherever possible. Differences were discussed openly and not settled by force.

marking_scheme.step: Compromise and accommodation; consensus wherever possible

questions.stem_md: An imagined clause of Zandria gives every adult a vote, and another fixes a fair wage. Name the form of justice each of them serves.
questions.solution_md: Political and economic justice.

answer.model_answer_md: The clause giving every adult a **vote** serves **political justice**, because it gives each person a voice in public affairs. The clause fixing a **fair wage** serves **economic justice**, since it concerns fairness in livelihood.

questions.stem_md: List any six features of the political philosophy of the Indian Constitution as set out in the textbook.
questions.solution_md: Any six features.

answer.model_answer_md: Features include **individual freedom**, **social justice**, **respect for diversity and minority rights**, **secularism of the Indian kind**, **universal adult franchise**, **federalism**, including special provisions for some states, and **one national identity** beside regional and other identities. Any six may be listed.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Delvar sets aside seats in public colleges for communities that were shut out of schooling for generations. Explain how this scheme can be seen as social justice.
questions.solution_md: Link the scheme with equality of opportunity.

answer.model_answer_md: Communities shut out of schooling for generations **start behind** others. Setting aside seats gives them a **fair chance** to compete, which is **equality of opportunity**. The Constitution allows such **special provisions**, including reservations for **Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes**, as a means to social justice.

marking_scheme.step: Long exclusion has left some groups behind
Seats give a fair chance: equality of opportunity
Reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as a means to social justice

questions.stem_md: Compare, in brief, the Western model of secularism, as a strict separation of state and religion, with the Indian model.
questions.solution_md: Two models compared.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **Western model**, the state and religion are kept **strictly apart**, with little intervention and no state support for religious bodies. The **Indian model** instead has the state hold a **principled distance** from every religion, while it may **step in to reform**, as against untouchability, or give **equal support** to all communities.

marking_scheme.step: Indian model: principled distance from all religions
Intervention for reform and equal support

questions.stem_md: Some critics say that the Constituent Assembly was not representative. State the ground of the criticism and the reply that is commonly given.
questions.solution_md: Criticism and reply.

answer.model_answer_md: Critics have argued that the Assembly was **elected on a limited franchise**, and not by universal adult franchise, so it did not speak for everyone. The reply is that its members held **diverse opinions** and that its **debates were open**, so many views were heard.

marking_scheme.step: Ground: elected on a limited franchise

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Lakemoor School a student says the Constitution is too long to be useful. State this criticism by its name and give the reply that another student could offer.
questions.solution_md: Name and reply.

answer.model_answer_md: The criticism is that the Constitution is **unwieldy**: very long and detailed. A reply is that the length **reflects the needs of India**, a large and diverse country, and that **much detail** is usual in constitutions, since it spells out powers and rights clearly.

marking_scheme.step: The criticism named: unwieldy, long and detailed
Reply: reflects the needs of India

questions.stem_md: State three limitations of the Constitution that the textbook notes.
questions.solution_md: The three limitations.

answer.model_answer_md: The textbook notes three limitations. First, a **centralised notion of national unity**, which some critics find too reliant on strong Union powers. Second, matters of **gender justice**, for instance inside the family, were **left partly unaddressed**. Third, certain **social and economic rights** appear in the **Directive Principles** rather than among the Fundamental Rights.

marking_scheme.step: Gender justice within the family not fully addressed
Some social and economic rights in the Directive Principles

questions.stem_md: Explain the criticism that the Constitution is alien and the reply to it.
questions.solution_md: The criticism and the reply.

answer.model_answer_md: Critics have argued that the Constitution is **alien** because many of its provisions were **borrowed** from other countries. The reply is that borrowed ideas were **adapted to Indian conditions** and to the **ideals of the national movement**, so the document is not a mere copy.

marking_scheme.step: Reply: in line with ideals of the national movement

questions.stem_md: Explain the ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity as they appear in the Preamble.
questions.solution_md: Four ideals with their meanings.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Justice** has three forms: **social, economic and political**.
2. **Liberty** covers freedom of **thought, expression, belief, faith and worship**.
3. **Equality** means equality of **status** and of **opportunity**, that is, equal standing and a fair chance.
4. **Fraternity** assures the **dignity of the individual**.
5. It also assures the **unity and integrity of the nation**.
6. Together these ideals show the values the Constitution wishes to realise.

marking_scheme.step: Equality of status and of opportunity
Fraternity: unity and integrity of the nation

questions.stem_md: Describe the core features of the political philosophy of the Indian Constitution as given in the textbook.
questions.solution_md: Seven features in brief.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Individual freedom**, for example freedom of expression and protection against arbitrary arrest.
2. **Social justice**, including reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
3. **Respect for diversity and minority rights**, with community-based rights beside individual rights.
4. The **Indian model of secularism**, a principled distance from all religions.
5. **Universal adult franchise** from the start, and **federalism** with special provisions for some states.
6. **One national identity** beside other identities.

marking_scheme.step: Federalism with special provisions, and national identity

questions.stem_md: How do respect for diversity, minority rights, federalism and the idea of national identity together reflect the philosophy of the Constitution?
questions.solution_md: Four features linked by unity in diversity.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The Constitution **respects diversity** and recognises **community-based rights**, such as the right of minorities to run educational institutions.
2. **Federalism** gives regions their own governments.
3. **Special provisions for some states** show asymmetric arrangements that suit particular needs.
4. **One national identity** is affirmed beside regional, linguistic and religious identities.
5. Together they show that **unity and diversity** are meant to go together, so that belonging to the nation does not need uniformity.

marking_scheme.step: Respect for diversity and community-based rights

questions.stem_md: Critics have argued that the Constitution is unwieldy, unrepresentative and alien. State each criticism with the reply, and say which reply seems to you the stronger, giving a reason.
questions.solution_md: Three criticisms, three replies and a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Unwieldy**: it is very long and detailed. Reply: its length **reflects India's needs**, and **much detail** is usual.
2. **Unrepresentative**: the Assembly was elected on a **limited franchise**. Reply: members stood for **many different opinions**, and **open debate** was the rule.
3. **Alien**: many provisions were **borrowed**. Reply: they were **adapted** to Indian conditions and the **ideals of the national movement**.
4. A student may find one reply stronger, for example the third, **with a reason** such as the adaptation of borrowed ideas.

marking_scheme.step: A reason given for the choice

questions.stem_md: Discuss the limitations of the Constitution that are noted in the textbook, and say how each may be weighed.
questions.solution_md: Three limitations with a weighing of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Some critics see a **centralised notion of national unity**; others reply that a strong sense of unity was needed.
2. Some issues of **gender justice**, such as those **within the family**, were **not fully addressed**.
3. Some **social and economic rights** were placed in the **Directive Principles** instead of the Fundamental Rights, so a citizen cannot claim them in court.
4. A student should **weigh** each limitation with reasons and with the Constitution's achievements.

marking_scheme.step: Rights placed in the Directive Principles
Another view or reply on at least one limitation
A reasoned weighing, not a one-sided verdict

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the philosophy of the Constitution? Explain how a constitution can transform a society and also limit power, and state the procedural achievements of the Assembly.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, two roles and procedure.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **philosophy of the Constitution** is the set of **ideals and moral values** behind its provisions.
2. A constitution can be a **means of democratic transformation**, by ending old exclusions through lawful means.
3. It can also **limit power**, by binding those who govern.
4. Its making shows **faith in deliberation** and a **spirit of compromise**.
5. Decisions were taken by **consensus** wherever possible.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning of the philosophy of a constitution

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Freedom to hold and share opinions is liberty.

**(b)** A decent wage concerns fairness in livelihood.

**(c) (i)** Fraternity and its two assurances.

**OR (c) (ii)** Equality of opportunity.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Liberty** of thought and expression.

**(b)** **Economic justice**.

**(c) (i)** Clause 4 expresses **fraternity**. By promoting a feeling of **belonging together**, it protects the **unity and integrity of the nation** and the **dignity of every community**.

**OR (c) (ii)** Clause 3 expresses **equality of opportunity**. A place in a public school gives the child a **fair chance to develop** and to compete, whatever the **community of birth**.

questions.stem_md: Read the table from an imagined handbook and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined handbook written by SOYL for practice; Veldora and Tarsia are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** It gives no funds and never steps in.

**(b)** It supports faiths equally and may reform.

**(c) (i)** Equal support and intervention for reform.

**OR (c) (ii)** One reason for, one for caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Veldora**.

**(b)** **Tarsia**.

**(c) (i)** The state gives **equal support** to the institutions of all faiths, and it may **intervene by law** to end practices that deny equality, as the Indian state did against **untouchability**.

**OR (c) (ii)** Such a society may prefer it because the state can **reform practices that deny equality**. Some urge caution because **intervention** might be **misused** or could affect the freedom of a community to manage its own religious affairs.

children.solution_md: It gives no funds and never steps in.

answer.model_answer_md: **Veldora**.

children.stem_md: Whose approach is closer to the Indian model of secularism?
children.solution_md: It supports faiths equally and may reform.
